packets.key_finding: Shrouding the autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, since nudged users mostly chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum, and missed payments increased.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with a six-month follow-up on payment behavior.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a nudge intervention can move an enrollment-adjacent metric while leaving the substantive outcome unchanged and even worsening some behaviors — direct support for the team's concern that headline enrollment could be a vanity metric for round-up savings.
limitations: Studies credit-card minimum-payment nudging, not a savings round-up feature
Only 6-month follow-up, not 12 months
Mechanism (shrouding an option) differs from opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing
packets.relevance_reason: Direct consumer financial product evidence that a default/nudge can shift enrollment-like metrics without moving the outcome that matters, speaking to the brief's amount-vs-nominal-enrollment question.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: A default nudge shifted investment risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes across five European countries, but lowered ratings of the advice given compared to no default, especially when the default was refused, with perceived advisor honesty mediating the effect.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative five-country European sample (n=4207), testing default nudges and framing of default presentation in investment decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial default reads as manipulative to European consumers, informing how the round-up entry screen should be framed to avoid a dark-pattern perception while still capturing enrollment.
limitations: Wealth-management/investment risk context rather than round-up savings
Effect on longer-term behavior not reported, only immediate choice and advice rating
Abstract gives effect sizes qualitatively (medium-to-large), not exact numbers
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-decision experiment addressing exactly when a default is perceived as manipulative, squarely the dark-pattern/reputational risk the brief flags.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage on iOS rose 113% and on Android 12% relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still present 15 months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of DMA-mandated choice screens on iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct, long-horizon (15-month) evidence that an EU-mandated active-choice screen produces large, persistent behaviour change without a default — the clearest real-world test of whether active choice captures meaningful benefit versus a default, exactly what the entry-mechanism decision needs.
limitations: mobile browser choice, not a financial enrolment or savings decision
platform-level usage share, not individual engagement or amount outcomes
packets.relevance_reason: The most directly relevant recent evidence on active/forced choice versus defaults in a mobile app context under EU regulation, with unusually long follow-up.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework showing that whether default effects persist downstream depends on the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review synthesizing prior default-effect literature into a taxonomy and research agenda.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a structured account of which conditions make a default's enrollment effect persist versus fade, directly informing what to measure and watch for when tracking round-up enrollment at 6-12 months.
limitations: Conceptual/theoretical, no new empirical effect sizes
Not specific to financial products
Abstract gives no concrete numbers
packets.relevance_reason: A recent, general framework specifically about when default effects persist versus wash out downstream, matching the brief's persistence and heterogeneity questions.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Automatic enrollment raises steady-state saving rates by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by only 0.3%, as job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs (only 40% escalate on the first date) erode the headline effect.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative statement of the support team's objection: the enrollment lift from a default is real at signup but much smaller in steady state once turnover and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: Retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
Nine firm-level 401(k) plans, may not generalize
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, directly answering the brief's amount-vs-nominal-enrollment question.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43M but also increased requested refunds by almost $3M, with larger effects on smaller and first-time donors who likely did not intend the recurring commitment.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences causal design across political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
packets.why_it_matters: Real-world evidence that a recurring-contribution default both lifts nominal sign-up and generates unwanted commitments and refund/complaint behaviour, mirroring exactly the support team's concern about passively-enrolled users regretting the round-up feature.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
measures refunds as a complaint proxy rather than direct satisfaction or withdrawal data
packets.relevance_reason: Directly evidences the trade-off the brief asks about: a default that increases nominal enrolment/amount while also increasing complaint-like behaviour, with clear heterogeneity by donor experience and size.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together; removing either friction alone would not sustain adherence, and adding a lower tip-menu option captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey of consumer preferences.
packets.why_it_matters: Decomposes exactly why a preset menu option anchors choice into two separable, manipulable frictions — a technique directly transferable to designing the round-up multiplier menu and calibrating how easy opting out should be, and it shows adding an intermediate option can raise welfare cheaply.
limitations: Setting is taxi tipping menus, not financial savings
One-time transactional choice rather than a recurring savings decision
US urban context, not EU
packets.relevance_reason: The friction-decomposition method (deviation cost vs. opt-out cost) is an explicit, transferable technique for designing preset-menu defaults and predicting anchoring on the round-up multiplier.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrolment into just-in-time text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, though this captures less than half of avoidable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks measuring real transaction outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for auto-enrolling bank customers (not employees) into a beneficial default feature and measuring genuine behavioural savings, directly supporting the case for opt-out enrolment in a banking app.
limitations: studies alert/notification enrolment rather than a savings pot enrolment or contribution-level decision
no anchoring or multi-year persistence data given
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer-financial, self-directed, bank-app setting with a real automatic-enrolment default and measured downstream financial outcomes — the closest analogue to the brief's own product.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: A comprehensive review of household finance summarizing empirical regularities in savings, borrowing, and asset allocation and the interventions (choice architecture, product design, disclosure, defaults) firms and governments use to shape financial behavior, alongside behavioral explanations for deviations from the classical model.
packets.methodology: Narrative/synthesis review chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: The synthesis source for weighing default and choice-architecture interventions against product-design and disclosure alternatives across the household-finance literature, useful for calibrating expectations before committing to a specific enrollment design.
limitations: broad overview without a single headline effect size specific to round-up savings
covers many financial domains beyond enrollment defaults, diluting specificity
abstract-only, no numeric findings given
packets.relevance_reason: Serves as the review/synthesis anchor giving broader context on choice architecture and defaults across consumer financial behavior, satisfying the brief's need for a review with effect sizes across the literature.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A randomized nudge (payment reminders) in a Brazilian financial-management app cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who already had overdraft histories experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Field experiment (RCT) with a financial management platform in Brazil, comparing users randomized to receive payment reminders versus not, tracking fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern about heterogeneous harm from choice-architecture interventions: a nudge that helps most users on average can net-harm a vulnerable subgroup, which is exactly the distributional check needed before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or contribution-level presets
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a savings sweep product
no data on multi-month enrollment persistence or contribution amounts
packets.relevance_reason: Provides rare experimental evidence of a nudge with heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects in a consumer fintech setting, speaking directly to the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' question.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' policies (forcing a yes/no decision with no default) can be as effective as automatic enrollment at motivating behavior change, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant — which highlights losses from the non-preferred option — further improves on plain active choice; the authors recommend it as a complement to, or substitute for, automatic enrollment including in savings behavior contexts.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel 'enhanced active choice' design against opt-out defaults, drawing on savings-behavior policy examples as well as health care.
alternates.why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the brief's central open question — whether active choice captures most of the enrollment benefit without the disengagement/manipulation cost of opt-out — and offers a concrete enhanced-active-choice design (framing the forgone option as a loss) that could be built into onboarding.
limitations: primary field experiments are in medication adherence, not financial products
no long-term (6–12 month) persistence data reported
savings behavior application is discussed by analogy/reference rather than tested directly in this paper's own experiments
alternates.relevance_reason: Explicitly proposes and tests active choice / enhanced active choice as an alternative entry mechanism to automatic enrollment, naming savings behavior as an application domain — directly actionable for Decision 1.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians found people generally approve of financial nudges (rating them positively on approval, benefit, ethics, and likelihood-of-use), with strong preference for System 2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messaging, while transparency had no significant effect on ratings.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, representative Australian sample (n=2,100), varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly informs the dark-pattern/manipulation risk question: it suggests savings-framed, reflective (System 2, active-choice-like) interventions are rated more favourably and that disclosing mechanism (transparency) does not hurt approval, which should shape how the round-up entry and level are framed and communicated to users.
limitations: measures stated approval of hypothetical scenarios, not actual enrollment or savings behaviour
not specific to a round-up savings product or app onboarding flow
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer evidence on when a financial nudge is perceived as helpful versus manipulative, central to the EU dark-pattern concern in the brief.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from EU-law-relevant dark patterns, mapping existing EU statutes onto it.
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy construction; abstract-only, no empirical data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete framework for testing whether a pre-ticked opt-out enrolment or a pre-selected multiplier would read as manipulative under EU law, directly bearing on the entry-mechanism choice and its reputational risk.
limitations: purely doctrinal/legal, no behavioural or effect-size data
not specific to financial products, covers online choice architecture generally
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the opt-out design.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Derives a general characterization of optimal default design showing that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, a form of weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to externalities, fees, and designer-chooser disagreement.
alternates.methodology: Theoretical/analytical model of optimal default design using asymptotic approximations, verified by numerical simulation.
alternates.why_it_matters: Provides a formal decision rule for when an opt-out default is genuinely welfare-improving rather than merely enrollment-maximizing, bearing directly on whether the round-up feature should default users in and under what alignment-of-interest conditions that choice is defensible.
limitations: Purely theoretical/simulation-based, no empirical validation in a financial or consumer setting
Requires an argued assumption about whether designer and chooser interests align for round-up savings
Does not treat active choice as a distinct third design option
alternates.relevance_reason: A normative framework for when an opt-out default is truly optimal versus merely convenient for the firm, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision and the manipulation-risk question.
alternates.title: Optimal default options
alternates.abstract: Previous studies of optimal default options demonstrate that either opt-out minimization or maximization is optimal under restrictive conditions. We obtain a general characterization of the solution by studying optimal defaults when one of the problem’s parameters approaches a limiting value. We interpret these “asymptotic optima” as approximate optima for non-limiting cases and justify this interpretation through numerical simulations. When the designer and choosers agree about the activity’s value, simple forms of weighted opt-out minimization are asymptotically optimal. Additional results encompass Pigouvian fees, normative ambiguity, and cases in which the designer and choosers disagree about the activity’s value. • A general characterization of the optimal default options is provided. • The method used involves studying asymptotic optima as approximations. • With no externalities, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal. • The accuracy of the approximations is verified through simulations. • Extensions include cases with externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative ambiguity.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, automatic (passive) employer contributions increased total wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies mainly shifted assets between accounts, raising total saving by only about 1 cent per $1 spent, because roughly 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily swayed by automatic contributions.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data (41 million observations) on the full Danish population, comparing active-choice subsidy responses versus passive automatic-contribution responses.
alternates.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that passive defaults change real savings amounts, not just nominal enrollment, while active-choice mechanisms mainly cause account-shifting rather than new saving — directly bears on whether opt-out enrollment would produce genuine incremental round-up saving versus vanity enrollment.
limitations: retirement savings/subsidy context rather than liquid consumer round-up savings
passive vs active mechanism is about contribution rates set by employer, not user-chosen levels in an app
no measure of withdrawal or disengagement over time within the passive group
alternates.relevance_reason: Landmark large-sample evidence distinguishing whether defaults move actual saved amounts or merely reallocate existing assets, precisely the question the brief poses about enrollment versus real saving.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.
